#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Community Survey (ACS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The American Community Survey (ACS) is an ongoing nationwide survey conducted by the Census Bureau that collects vital information about the social, economic, housing, and demographic characteristics of our nation's population. Replacing the long form of the decennial census, the ACS is distributed to approximately 3.5 million addresses annually, providing detailed data throughout the year. Since 2005, it has generated estimates for areas with populations of 65,000 or more and, through 5-year accumulations, for smaller geographic areas such as census tracts and block groups. This data plays a crucial role in informing policy decisions and guiding the distribution of trillions of dollars in federal funds each year.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/acs

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Community Survey (ACS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The American Community Survey (ACS) is an ongoing nationwide survey conducted by the Census Bureau that collects vital information about the social, economic, housing, and demographic characteristics of our nation's population. Replacing the long form of the decennial census, the ACS is distributed to approximately 3.5 million addresses annually, providing detailed data throughout the year. Since 2005, it has generated estimates for areas with populations of 65,000 or more and, through 5-year accumulations, for smaller geographic areas such as census tracts and block groups. This data plays a crucial role in informing policy decisions and guiding the distribution of trillions of dollars in federal funds each year.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/acs

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# American Community Survey (ACS): Research Report

## Summary

Your description is mostly accurate, but three parts need correcting or qualifying:

1. **"Trillions of dollars."** The usual source is a Census Bureau paper that counted 353 federal assistance programs distributing more than $2.8 trillion in fiscal year 2021 (FY2021) using "Decennial Census Programs data." That category combines the decennial census, the ACS, and the geographic programs that support both. The ACS is not credited alone, and FY2021 included large one-time pandemic programs. The Bureau's own wording, "helps inform how trillions of dollars… are distributed," is accurate. Saying the ACS by itself "guides" $2.8 trillion goes further than the source.
2. **"Since 2005" covers two different products.** 1-year estimates for areas of 65,000+ people start with the 2005 data year and were first released in 2006. The first 5-year estimates for tracts and block groups (2005–2009) did not appear until December 2010. Your description also leaves out two other products: the 1-year Supplemental Estimates (areas of 20,000+, starting with the 2014 data year) and the 3-year estimates, which were discontinued.
3. **The 3.5 million figure is correct**, with some detail. About 3.54 million housing-unit addresses are sampled each year, phased in during 2011–2012. From 2005 to 2010 the figure was about 2.9 million. That number is addresses sampled, not completed interviews. Group quarters (college dorms, prisons, nursing homes) are sampled separately, and Puerto Rico has its own Puerto Rico Community Survey with about 36,000 addresses.

The URL works. The full form is https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs.

---

## 1. Publisher and governance

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, part of the Department of Commerce. The ACS is funded within the Bureau's "Periodic Censuses and Programs" account and treated as part of the decennial census program. That makes it vulnerable when 2030 Census costs rise.
- **Budget:** The Congressional Research Service reports $250.9 million for the ACS in FY2023. The largest line item is in-person follow-up with households that don't respond.
- **Content oversight:** Questions must be justified by federal agencies' legal or program needs. They are reviewed through an Office of Management and Budget (OMB)-led interagency committee and approved under the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3506–3507).
- **Companion survey:** The Puerto Rico Community Survey asks the same questions with local adjustments.

## 2. Legal authority

- **Constitution:** Article I, Section 2 requires a census every ten years "in such Manner as [Congress] shall by Law direct."
- **Title 13 U.S.C. §141** authorizes the decennial census and "such other census information as necessary," including sampling. **§193** authorizes extra surveys. In 2002 the Government Accountability Office (GAO) concluded that Commerce has authority to run the ACS under §§141 and 193 (opinion B-289852). GAO also noted that no law specifically required the Bureau to create the ACS. The Bureau built it on its own initiative, and Congress funded it under the name "continuous measurement."
- **Mandatory response, §221:** The statute sets fines of up to $100 for refusing and $500 for false answers. Under general federal sentencing law (18 U.S.C. 3571) these can reach $5,000. In practice they are almost never enforced. GAO found no other federal household survey that is both mandatory and this detailed.
- **Confidentiality, §9:** Responses may be used only for statistical purposes. Nothing may be published that identifies a person, and only sworn Census employees may see individual responses. Copies are immune from legal process.
- **Court challenges:** In *Morales v. Evans* (2000), the court upheld the 2000 long-form questions against First, Fourth, and Fifth Amendment claims.

## 3. History

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1940–2000 | A "long form" went to a sample of households at each census. In 2000 that was about 1 in 6. |
| Early 1980s–1990s | Statistician Leslie Kish proposed "rolling samples." The Bureau developed the idea as "Continuous Measurement." |
| 1996 | First field tests in a few counties. |
| 1999–2004 | Expanded to test sites. The Census 2000 Supplementary Survey and later national tests showed the approach worked. |
| 2002 | GAO legal-authority opinion. |
| 2005 | Full rollout for housing units, about 2.9–3 million addresses a year. |
| 2006 | Group quarters added. First 1-year estimates (2005 data). |
| 2008 | First 3-year estimates (2005–2007). New questions on health insurance, marital history, and veterans' service-connected disability. |
| 2010 | First census with no long form. First 5-year estimates (2005–2009) released in December. |
| 2011–12 | Sample raised to 3.54 million addresses. |
| 2012 | The House voted to defund the ACS and make it voluntary. The measure was not enacted. |
| 2013 | Online response option added, plus questions on computer and internet use. |
| 2015 | 3-year estimates dropped after budget cuts. The last was 2011–2013. Supplemental 1-year estimates began with 2014 data. |
| 2017 | Telephone follow-up interviewing stopped. |
| 2020 | The pandemic disrupted data collection, and the housing-unit response rate fell to 71.2%. Standard 2020 1-year estimates were not released. "Experimental" estimates were published instead. |
| 2023 | Administrative records began to be used to decide which in-person follow-up cases to stop pursuing. |
| 2025 | Gender-identity work was suspended under Executive Order 14168. The 2024 1-year estimates came out on September 11, 2025. The fall 2025 government shutdown delayed later releases. |
| Jan 29, 2026 | 2020–2024 5-year estimates released, the first time there are four non-overlapping 5-year datasets. 5-year Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) files were scheduled for March 5, 2026. |

## 4. Methods and data products

- **Collection:** Each address has about a 1-in-480 chance of selection each month and should not be picked more than once in five years. Households respond online or by mail. Some non-responding households are then sampled for in-person or phone visits by field staff. The survey covers more than 40 topics and supports over 300 federal uses.
- **Products:**
  - 1-year estimates for areas of 65,000+
  - 1-year Supplemental Estimates for areas of 20,000+
  - 5-year estimates down to tracts and block groups
  - PUMS (Public Use Microdata Sample) files for geographic areas of at least 100,000 people
  - Variance replicate estimates
  - Special tabulations, such as citizen voting-age population by race and ethnicity for Voting Rights Act work
  - Restricted microdata through the Federal Statistical Research Data Centers
- **Estimates cover a period, not a point in time.** They are weighted to match the Bureau's Population Estimates Program totals. Every estimate comes with a margin of error.

## 5. Data quality trends that matter to users

Housing-unit response rates: 97.6% (2011), 95.8% (2015), 92.0% (2018), 86.0% (2019), 71.2% (2020), 85.3% (2021), 84.7% (2023), 82.9% (2024).

Refusals rose from about 1–2% to 9.5%. The Bureau says lower response in the 2020s raises the risk of nonresponse bias. It published a research note on unexpected year-to-year changes in the 2024 1-year data and said it found no collection or processing errors. Advocates argue that years of underfunding have kept the sample from growing and margins of error from shrinking.

## 6. Users and uses

- **Federal:**
  - HUD: Fair Market Rents and the CHAS housing-needs data
  - Justice Department: Voting Rights Act §203 language-assistance decisions, and citizen voting-age population data for redistricting and enforcement
  - Education: Title I, via the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE)
  - Veterans' job-training allocations
  - Transportation planning
  - Benchmarking for other federal surveys
- **State, local, and tribal governments:** planning for schools, roads, hospitals, and emergency management; grant applications; needs assessments.
- **Business:** site selection, market analysis, survey sampling frames.
- **Researchers, journalists, nonprofits, and advocates:** poverty, income, housing burden, language, disability, commuting, migration, health insurance, and civil-rights enforcement. It is the only source of local statistics for most of its topics.

## 7. Public benefits

- It provides yearly data, instead of once a decade, for every community, including small and rural areas.
- It supports funding formulas, eligibility rules, compliance monitoring, and anti-discrimination enforcement.
- It is a free public good that supports a large commercial and nonprofit analytics industry.

## 8. Access points

**Official:**
- data.census.gov (American FactFinder was retired in 2020)
- Census Data API
- Summary File (table-based format)
- FTP site at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/
- TIGER/Line boundary files
- Documentation: the Design and Methodology Report, the yearly "Accuracy of the Data," subject definitions, user notes, and errata

**Third-party and mirrors:**
- IPUMS USA (harmonized microdata) and NHGIS (University of Minnesota)
- ICPSR
- Census Reporter, Social Explorer, PolicyMap
- R packages tidycensus and censusapi; Python package cenpy
- Data.gov catalog entries

## 9. Preservation notes for archivists

- **Risk:** In early 2025, parts of census.gov were briefly taken offline to remove gender-identity content. The Williams Institute counts about 360 federal data collections that have dropped sexual orientation or gender identity measures. Senate appropriators asked the Bureau to explain the removal of Census and Bureau of Economic Analysis datasets and the ending of its advisory committees.
- **What to capture:**
  - Each year's Summary Files and PUMS for 1-year, 5-year, and the discontinued 3-year products
  - Variance replicate files
  - Questionnaires by year
  - Code lists and data dictionaries
  - Errata and user notes
  - Geography files matched to each data year (2020 tract changes; Connecticut's planning regions replacing counties in the 2022 data)
  - 2020 experimental files
  - Methodology reports
- **Integrity:** Record release dates and errata. The Bureau sometimes reissues tables.

## 10. Policy debates

- **Mandatory vs. voluntary response.** Congress defunded the ACS in a 2012 House vote. A House rider (FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science bill, Section 605) would have blocked enforcement and limited follow-ups to two contacts. The final FY2026 agreement dropped it and gave the Bureau about $1.5 billion. I could not confirm whether that agreement was signed into law, so check before citing it.
- **Privacy and respondent burden.** Critics object to intrusive questions. Formal privacy methods like those used for the 2020 Census have been studied for the ACS but not adopted.
- **Content.** Sexual orientation and gender identity questions were funded and tested for possible use from 2027, then suspended in 2025. OMB revised its race and ethnicity standards in 2024 (combined question, a Middle Eastern or North African category); how that will be carried out is uncertain. A 2023 proposal to change the disability questions was withdrawn after public objections.
- **Funding.** Advocates such as The Census Project are asking for an extra $100–300 million to restore and enhance the ACS.

## 11. Practical tips for analysts

- Always report margins of error.
- Don't compare overlapping 5-year periods.
- Don't treat 2020 1-year data as standard.
- Adjust dollar figures for inflation.
- Watch for geography boundary changes and population-control revisions.
- Use 1-year data for timeliness and 5-year data for precision and small areas.

---

**Main sources:** census.gov ACS pages (Information Guide, response rates, release schedules, 2024 research note), ACS Design and Methodology Report (2022), GAO opinion B-289852, CRS IN12303 and IF12714, Census working paper on FY2021 federal funds, U.S. Code Title 13, The Census Project, NPR, AP, KFF, and the Williams Institute.

# ACS Risk Assessment (as of early October 2026)

ACS data that has already been published looks safe. The risk is to new data, which will likely be later and less detailed. The main reason is a Commerce Department order from June 2026, DAO 216-26 ("Disclosure Avoidance for Statistical Products"). It bans "noise infusion," a set of privacy-protection methods (including record swapping and synthetic data) that the ACS has long relied on. As a result, the 2025 1-year estimates, normally published in mid-September, have been delayed with no release date. The Census Bureau's leadership change and staff losses add to the risk.

**Corrections to my previous report:**
- The FY2026 appropriation was enacted. ACS funding is $210.9M in FY2026, down from $240.9M in FY2025.
- George Cook, a Commerce Department political appointee, replaced the career acting director Ron Jarmin in September 2025. Jarmin retired on May 15, 2026.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for higher risk:**
- In early 2025, parts of census.gov were briefly taken offline to remove gender-identity content (covered in my previous report). That was a site-wide action, not aimed at ACS data.
- The Census Project and the Association of Public Data Users (APDU) worry about broader data removals. Senate appropriators asked the Bureau to explain removed Census and Bureau of Economic Analysis datasets.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The 2020–2024 5-year tables (January 29, 2026) and 5-year microdata files (March 5, 2026) were published normally. They are available through data.census.gov, the API and the FTP site.
- Cook's August 17, 2026 blog post says DAO 216-26 "applies only to new products going forward. Products that have already been published, such as the 2020 Census or the 2024 [ACS], won't be affected."
- I found no reports of ACS files or variables from earlier years being removed or changed. The gender-identity questions were only ever in a test (the 2024 Methods Panel), never in published ACS data, so cancelling that test removed nothing from existing data.
- Full copies exist at IPUMS, NHGIS, ICPSR and elsewhere.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** Archivists should still capture the files from before the DAO now. They are the last ACS products made with the old privacy methods and will be the baseline for checking future changes.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- The 2025 1-year estimates missed their usual mid-September date. The Bureau calls the delay open-ended: "release date… is being determined… later this year" (Census press release, August 4, 2026; ACS updates page). The Ohio Capital Journal (October 2, 2026) says it is the first time since the ACS began in 2005 that the 1-year release didn't happen on schedule.
- More than 100 organizations, led by The Census Project, wrote to Commerce Secretary Lutnick on September 4, 2026 about the "indefinite delay."
- Later products depend on this one. The 5-year release, usually in December, and HUD income limits may slip too (Novogradac, September 8, 2026). APDU says 5-year data "will start to see impacts this year."

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- Collection continues. The ACS's paperwork clearance (OMB control number 0607-0810) was renewed September 23, 2025 and runs until June 30, 2027. A revision for 2027 is in progress: comment notices ran December 19, 2025 and May 2026 (91 FR 27241).
- No law sets a publication deadline, and no year has been skipped yet. The Bureau still says it intends to release the data "later this year."
- The 2020–2024 5-year release was pushed from December 2025 to January 2026 by the government shutdown.

**Rating: Moderate Risk, close to High.** A delayed release is exactly what the Moderate level describes. If the 2025 1-year data hasn't appeared by early 2027, or the 2021–2025 5-year release is pushed back as well, this should move to High.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- DAO 216-26 allows only "coarsening" (rounding, grouping values into ranges, merging small areas into larger ones) and suppression (withholding data).
  - Cook's blog says these "can reduce the amount and detail of data published, especially for small geographic areas or population groups."
  - The Tennessee State Data Center says this "will almost certainly mean less granular data or fewer published tables."
  - The Census Project expects severe effects on small-area and rural statistics.
- Timeliness has already suffered, since the 2025 1-year release is late.
- The changeover will run through 2029. The 2021–2025 5-year release will mix one year under the new rules with four years under the old ones, which creates a break in the time series.
- Response rates keep falling: 97.6% in 2011, 86.0% in 2019, 82.9% in 2024. Refusals have risen to about 9.5%.
- Field staffing is short. The Commerce Inspector General (OIG-25-013-I) found a 17% average shortfall in ACS field interviewers over FY2019–2023.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The full scale of lost detail isn't known yet. Implementation guidelines are still being written.
- Sample size (about 3.54M addresses) and questionnaire content are unchanged. The 2026 questionnaire is the same as 2025.

**Rating: High Risk.** Timeliness has already been lost, and the Bureau itself says detail and granularity will be reduced.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for higher risk:**
- No statute names the ACS. In 2002 the Government Accountability Office (opinion B-289852) said no law required it to be created. It rests on general survey authority in Title 13 §§141 and 193.
- Congress has repeatedly tried to make responses voluntary or cut funding. Examples are the 2012 House defunding vote and Section 605 of the House FY2026 bill, which was dropped from the final law.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Title 13 §141 explicitly covers "such other census information as necessary," including sampling. Responding is mandatory (§221), and confidentiality is protected by law (§9).
- Many federal programs rely on it:
  - Census determinations of which jurisdictions must provide voting materials in other languages (Voting Rights Act §203)
  - HUD Fair Market Rents and income limits
  - Title I school funding, via the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates
  - More than 300 documented federal uses
  - Programs distributing more than $2.8T, a figure that covers census data generally (FY2021)
- Nothing else can substitute for it at the tract and county level.
- The Bureau's FY2027 budget justification calls the ACS "the premier source" and part of the decennial census program.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** The authority is somewhat general, but federal programs clearly need the data and nothing can replace it.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- About 1,300 Census employees left in 2025 through deferred resignation, early retirement and similar programs (the union AFGE Council 241, via AP and Government Executive). That is above the 1,000-staff threshold, out of about 13,230 employees in September 2024.
  - The American Statistical Association's "Nation's Data at Risk 2025" report estimates a 15% staff loss since FY2024.
  - The FY2026 request cut staff for the program area that includes the ACS (Periodic Censuses and Programs) by 27%.
- Leadership has been removed or replaced:
  - Director Robert Santos resigned in February 2025.
  - The career acting director Jarmin was replaced in September 2025 by George Cook, a political appointee who also holds Commerce leadership roles. Critics say he lacks the qualifications the director's statute requires (NPR, AP, CRS).
  - Jarmin retired in May 2026, and no replacement has been named.
  - AP reported 18 vacancies among top leaders and their staff.
- The ACS budget fell from $240.9M (FY2025) to $210.9M (FY2026), a 12.5% cut (COSSA, CRS R48929).
- The FY2027 request keeps the ACS flat. However, it cuts the separate Current Surveys and Programs account by 9.4%, and NACo warns that affects ongoing surveys.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The 1,300 figure is for the whole Bureau. I found no breakdown for ACS staff alone.
- The budget cut on its own (12.5%) would only reach the Moderate level.
- I couldn't get figures from the usajobs-tracker site. Its numbers load through JavaScript I couldn't run, and the site stopped updating on December 31, 2025.

**Rating: High Risk.** Both the staff-loss threshold (1,000 or more) and the leadership-removal criterion are met.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- DAO 216-26 (June 4, 2026) is a major policy change made in line with Administration priorities. It was issued without advance notice and states that "any use of noise infusion is inconsistent with the Department's policies." It directly caused the 2025 delay and will change ACS products through 2029.
- A presidential action changed ACS-related paperwork. Executive Order 14168 led the Bureau to cancel part of the ACS gender-identity test in January 2025 and to file a change with OMB to discontinue it (control number 0607-0936).
- A related proposed rule for the decennial census (September 10, 2026) reportedly cites disclosure avoidance as part of the reason for removing questions on race, ethnicity and sexual orientation (Community Solutions). I couldn't check this against the rule itself. If accurate, it suggests the ACS could face similar content proposals.
- Political leadership now runs the Bureau, and the FY2027 budget proposes reorganizing the federal statistical agencies.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- Some changes are proposed or still pending. The 2027 ACS revision would add the updated 2024 race/ethnicity question (OMB's Statistical Policy Directive No. 15) and an internet response option in Puerto Rico. Details of how the DAO will be carried out are still undetermined.

**Rating: High Risk.**

---

## Recommendations for preservationists
- Capture now all pre-DAO products: the 2024 1-year and 2020–2024 5-year tables, microdata (PUMS) and variance replicate files, plus their documentation.
- Record DAO 216-26 itself and the Bureau's implementation guidance.
- When the 2025 1-year data comes out, compare its tables and level of detail with 2024. That will show what was suppressed or coarsened.
